parsed.summary: This paper investigates systematic errors in neural morphological generation for Japanese past-tense verb inflection, focusing on rare morphological subclasses. It identifies a specific irregular subtype, Type 4-2 verbs, as disproportionately error-prone and demonstrates through controlled ablation experiments that removing this subtype improves model accuracy more than removing all irregular verbs combined. The study highlights the importance of fine-grained subclass analysis in morphological evaluation.

chk_problem.value: Neural morphological generation systems achieve high aggregate accuracy but fail systematically in rare morphological subclasses.
chk_problem.paper_quote: Neural morphological generation systems often achieve high aggregate accuracy on benchmark datasets, yet such performance can conceal systematic errors clustered in rare morphological subclasses.

chk_method.value: Orthography-aware diagnosis and causal isolation using controlled ablation experiments.
chk_method.paper_quote: We present an orthography-aware diagnosis of Japanese past-tense verb inflection, treating hiragana not merely as a transcriptional medium but as a representational system that encodes morphophonological structure.

chk_data.value: Japanese verb inflection dataset in morphological transduction format, converted to hiragana, with 3,958 verbs.
chk_data.paper_quote: We use a Japanese verb inflection dataset in standard morphological transduction format, following the setup of Vylomova et al. (2020) and Goldman et al. (2023).

chk_setup.value: Two character-level Transformer architectures (PGT and LST) trained on Japanese past-tense inflection data with five random seeds and eight ablation conditions.
chk_setup.paper_quote: We evaluate two character-level Transformer encoder–decoder architectures for Japanese past-tense inflection, both operating over hiragana strings and generating inflected forms autoregressively.

chk_primary_result.value: Type 4-2 verbs, comprising <1% of data, account for 30–43% of residual errors and contribute 34–48× their prevalence to total errors.
chk_primary_result.paper_quote: Using two character-level Transformer architectures evaluated across five random seeds, we show that although both systems exceed 97% aggregate accuracy, a single structurally specific irregular subtype, verbs whose stems end in /e/ and require gemination before the past-tense suffix and make up fewer than 1% of the data, accounts for a disproportionate 30–43% share of residual errors and contributes roughly 34–48× its prevalence to total errors.

chk_secondary_result.value: Removing Type 4-2 verbs alone improves accuracy more than removing all irregular verbs combined.
chk_secondary_result.paper_quote: Controlled ablation experiments show that removing this subtype alone produces larger accuracy gains than removing all irregular verbs combined.

chk_baseline.value: Baseline accuracy of 97.98% (PGT) and 97.73% (LST) on the full dataset.
chk_baseline.paper_quote: On the primary run, both systems achieve high aggregate accuracy on the full dataset: 97.98% (PGT) and 97.73% (LST).

chk_conclusion.value: Not all irregularity is equally destabilizing; fine-grained, subgroup-aware evaluation is necessary for morphological learning.
chk_conclusion.paper_quote: These results demonstrate that high aggregate accuracy can mask structurally localized failures, that not all irregularity is equally destabilizing to neural generalization, and that fine-grained, subgroup-aware evaluation is necessary to reveal and causally test such effects.

chk_limitation.value: Study focuses on a single language, paradigm, and two architectures; cross-linguistic validation and replication are needed.
chk_limitation.paper_quote: Cross-linguistic validation is necessary to determine whether comparable low-frequency structural subtypes produce similar disparities in other morphologically rich languages, and whether larger pretrained models exhibit different sensitivity to the patterns we identify.
